definition: Someone who is a detective.

definition: Taking full advantage of an opportunity while it lasts.

definition: The formation of blood cells in the living body (especially in the bone marrow).

definition: Markedly effective as if by emotional pressure.
example: Impelling skill as a teller of tales.

definition: In an imperative and commanding manner.
In an imperial manner.
example: Imperially decreed.

definition: Without warmth.
example: He treated his patients impersonally.

definition: Rash impulsiveness.
etymology: From English impetuous + -ity, from Middle French impétuosité, from Old French.

definition: In an impulsive or impetuous way; without taking cautions.
Difficult or impossible to evaluate with precision.
example: Such imponderable human factors as aesthetic sensibility.

definition: Persistent to the point of annoying.
etymology: First attested in 1477, in Middle english; from Latin importūnus + -ate (adjective-forming suffix), modelled on Middle French importuné. By surface analysis, importune + -ate (compare inopportune).

definition: Pretending to be another person.
etymology: From Middle French imposture, from Late Latin impostura, Latin impostus.

definition: In an imprecise manner.
example: He expressed himself imprecisely.

definition: Splendid or imposing in size or appearance.
example: Impressed by the richness of the flora.

definition: In an imprudent manner.
example: Imprudently, he downed tools and ran home to make his wife happy.

definition: A force that moves something along.
etymology: From Middle English impulsioun, from Old French impulsion, from Latin impulsio, impulsionem.

definition: In isolation and without reference to anything else.
example: The distillation is performed in vacuo to avoid decomposition of the compounds under study.

definition: Unacceptability as a consequence of not being admissible.
Not elegant or graceful in expression.
etymology: From French inapte, from Middle French, equivalent to in- + apt.

definition: Against which no argument can be made.
A lack of attentiveness (as to children or helpless people).
The phenomenon of light emission by a body as its temperature is raised.
etymology: Borrowed from French incandescence. Morphologically incandesce + -ence.

definition: Lacking in caution.
example: An incautious remark.

definition: Small hairless caterpillar having legs on only its front and rear segments; mostly larvae of moths of the family Geometridae.
etymology: From inch + worm. So called because their gradual movement seems to be measuring the ground; compare measuring worm.

definition: Make an incision into by carving or cutting.
In an incisive manner.
example: He was incisively critical.

definition: Impossible to measure or compare in value or size or excellence.
example: The side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable with each other; the diameter and circumference of a circle are incommensurable.
etymology: From Middle French incommensurable, from Medieval Latin incommensurabilis. Its full etymology is equivalent to that of in- + commensurable.

definition: The quality of being incomprehensible.
Not conclusively.
example: The meeting ended inconclusively.

definition: Without consideration; in an inconsiderate manner.
example: Inconsiderately, he asked to be invited for dinner.

definition: Unfaithfulness by virtue of being unreliable or treacherous.
example: Although she loved him for many years, his inconstancy eventually drove her to another.

definition: In an obvious and provable manner.
Free of corruption or immorality.
example: A policeman who was incorrupt and incorruptible.

definition: Teaching or impressing upon the mind by frequent instruction or repetition.
Showing absence of intellectual inquisitiveness or natural curiosity.
example: Strangely incurious about the cause of the political upheaval surrounding them.
etymology: From Latin incūriōsus (“careless”), from in- (“un-”) and cūriōsus (“careful”).

definition: Bent into or having an inward curve.
etymology: From in- + curved. Compare Latin incurvus.

definition: A small bone in the middle ear between the malleus and the stapes.
Lacking propriety and good taste in manners and conduct.
example: Indecorous behavior.
etymology: By surface analysis, in- + decorous; or, Latin indecōrus.

definition: With indefatigable energy.
example: She watched the show indefatigably.
etymology: From indefatigable + -ly, but indefatigable itself was attested later. In use since the 16th century.

definition: The strength to resist destruction.
Not capable of being definitely decided or ascertained.
etymology: From Middle French indeterminable, from Late Latin indeterminabilis.

definition: Of or relating to or serving as an index.
Without discretion or wisdom or self-restraint.
example: She inquired indiscreetly after the state of his health.

definition: (arithmetic) The state of being impossible to divide by a specific integer without leaving a remainder.
example: The primality of the number rests on the indivisibility of a certain quantity by that number.
etymology: From Middle French indivisibilité, from Ecclesiastical Latin indivisibilitas.

definition: Large short-tailed lemur of Madagascar having thick silky fur in black and white and fawn.
etymology: Possibly from Malagasy endrina (“the lemur Indri indri”).

definition: Too obvious to be doubted.
example: The indubitable effect of the potion convinced many nonbelievers.
etymology: Either from French indubitable or Latin indubitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + dubitable.

definition: In an industrious manner.
example: They hoed up weeds industriously all morning.

definition: Persevering determination to perform a task.
example: Frugality and industry are still regarded as virtues.

definition: Fill with sublime emotion.
example: He was inebriated by his phenomenal success.
etymology: From Latin inēbriō, inēbriāre, from ēbrius (“drunk”).

definition: To an inexpressible degree.
example: His songs are ineffably sweet and touching.

definition: In an ineffectual manner.
example: She tried ineffectually to light the primus, and Thomas came to help her.

definition: By necessity.
Immobility by virtue of being inert.
Lacking professional skill or expertise.
example: Inexpert but conscientious efforts.
etymology: From Middle English inexpert, inexperte, from in- (“not”) + expert, experte, or else from Middle French inexpert or its etymon Latin inexpertus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + expert.

definition: Not expressive.
example: An inexpressive face.

definition: An abnormal condition in which an older child or adult retains infantile characteristics.
example: A craniopharyngioma may produce infantilism.

definition: An essential auditory center in the midbrain.
An infinite quantity.
example: Euclid proved the infinitude of primes.
etymology: From Old French infinité, from Latin infinitas (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + finis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tas.

definition: Change the form of a word in accordance as required by the grammatical rules of the language.
example: The actress has a great skill of being able to inflect her voice to any situation.
etymology: From Latin īnflectō, from in- (“in”) + flectō (“to bend”).

definition: In an inflexible manner.
example: ‘You will — because you must!’ Madam told her inflexibly.

definition: A change in the form of a word (usually by adding a suffix) to indicate a change in its grammatical function.
etymology: From Middle French inflexion, itself from Latin īnflexiō.

definition: A monoclonal antibody (trade name Remicade) used to treat Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis; administered by infusion; use and dosage must be determined by a physician.
Flowing inward.
Having frequencies below those of audible sound.
Noteworthy scarcity.
example: The infrequency of her visits.
etymology: From Latin infrequentia (“scantiness”), equivalent to in- + frequency or infrequent + -cy.

definition: Something that grows inward.
example: Ingrowth is a common problem with toenails.

definition: The act of dwelling in or living permanently in a place (said of both animals and men).
example: He studied the creation and inhabitation and demise of the colony.

definition: Be inherent in something.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin inhaerēre (“stick in, stick to, inhere to”), from in (“in”) + haereō (“stick”); see hesitate. Compare adhere, cohere.

definition: Be part of.
example: This problem inheres in the design.

definition: The quality of being inhomogeneous.
The ritual placing of a corpse in a grave.
(computer science) the format of sectors on the surface of a hard disk drive so that the operating system can access them and setting a starting position.
A word formed from the initial letters of the several words in the name and pronounced as one word.
example: ‘NATO’ is an initialism for North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

definition: Lacking or showing lack of judgment or discretion; unwise.
example: An injudicious measure.

definition: A long, collared garment coming to the feet, with narrow, tapered sleeves, worn by all major and minor clergy, monastics, and often by male seminarians.
example: The inner rason is the basic garment, and is worn at all times, even when working.

definition: Originality by virtue of introducing new ideas.
A substance (a virus or toxin or immune serum) that is introduced into the body to produce or increase immunity to a particular disease.
A nucleoside that is formed by the deamination of adenosine; used in kidney transplantation to provide a temporary source of sugar.
etymology: From ἰνός (inós), genitive singular of ἴς (ís, “sinew, muscle”).

definition: An encroachment or intrusion.
example: They made inroads in the United States market.
etymology: The noun is derived from in + road (“(obsolete) act of riding on horseback; hostile ride against a particular area, raid”). The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: Not sanitary or healthful.
To an insatiable degree.
example: She was insatiably hungry.

definition: In a tentative and self-conscious manner.
example: She always acts very insecurely in the presence of her father.

definition: Devoid of feeling and consciousness and animation.
example: Insentient (or insensate) stone.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsēnsātus. By surface analysis, in- + sensate.

definition: A lack of sensibility.
etymology: From Old French insensibilité, from Late Latin insensibilitas.

definition: In an insensitive manner.
example: The police officer questioned the woman rather insensitively about the attack.

definition: In an insolent manner.
example: He had replied insolently to his superiors.

definition: Marked by blithe unconcern.
example: An utterly insouciant financial policy.
etymology: From French insouciant, from in- (“not”, prefix) + souciant (“worrying”), 1828.

definition: A leader who stimulates and excites people to action.
(medicine) blowing air or medicated powder into the lungs (or into some other body cavity).
An organized rebellion aimed at overthrowing a constituted government through the use of subversion and armed conflict.
A person who takes part in an armed rebellion against the constituted authority (especially in the hope of improving conditions).
The quality of being intangible and not perceptible by touch.
Of or relating to the integument.
The skin and its appendages.
In an intelligible manner.
example: The foreigner spoke to us quite intelligibly.

definition: Used of the set of attributes that distinguish the referents of a given word.
Having a day or month inserted to make the calendar year correspond to the solar year:.
example: A leap year is an intercalary year.
etymology: From Latin intercalārius, from intercalāris, from intercalō, from inter (“among”) + calō (“call out, proclaim”).

definition: A calendar year with an extra day added in February.
Mutual communication; communication with each other.
example: They intercepted intercommunication between enemy ships.

definition: A common language used by speakers of different languages.
example: Latin used to be the European interlanguage. Currently English widely serves this purpose.
etymology: From inter- + language. In the language acquisition sense introduced by Larry Selinker in 1972.

definition: Provide (books) with blank leaves.
The quality of being intermittent; subject to interruption or periodic stopping.
Learning (of values or attitudes etc.) that is incorporated within yourself.
Put under international control.
example: Internationalize trade of certain drugs.

definition: A person who is interned.
example: The internees were enemy aliens and suspected terrorists.

definition: A segment of a stem between two nodes.
The action of penetrating between or among.
Be or come between.
example: An interposing thicket blocked their way.
etymology: From Middle French interposer, influenced by poser (“to place, put”), from Latin interpōnō, from inter (“between”) + pōnō (“to place, put”).

definition: A measure of statistical dispersion, being equal to the difference between the upper and lower quartiles.
example: From the set of data above we have an interquartile range of 3.5, a range of 9 - 2 = 7 and a standard deviation of 2.34.

definition: Be in a relationship with.
Relating to the use of or having the nature of an interrogation.
example: An interrogatory glance.
etymology: From Late Latin; equivalent to interrogate + -ory (“pertaining to”), or more distantly inter- + rogatory.

definition: Used of competition or cooperation between secondary schools.
example: The interschool basketball tournament was held in March.

definition: Place at intervals in or among.
example: Intersperse exclamation marks in the text.

definition: (law) a party who interposes in a pending proceeding.
The situation of being or dying without a legally valid will.
Utter monotonously and repetitively and rhythmically.
example: To intone the church service.
etymology: From Middle English entune, entone, from Old French entoner, from Medieval Latin intonō, from in- (inchoative prefix) + tonus (“pitch, tone”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); doublet of intonate.

definition: The trait of being hard to influence or control.
Relating to areas between the layers of the skin.
example: An intradermal injection.

definition: An injection into the skin.
A form of skin test in which the suspected allergen is injected into the skin.
Within the system of ventricles in the brain.
example: Intraventricular pressure.

definition: A composition of vocal music that is appropriate for opening church services.
etymology: PIE word *h₁én From Late Middle English introite (“act of entering in or into, entrance;

definition: Aggressiveness as evidenced by intruding; by advancing yourself or your ideas without invitation.
Introduce a cannula or tube into.
example: The doctor is about to intubate the patient's trachea.
etymology: From in- + tube + -ate (verb-forming suffix). First appears c. 1612 in the publications of Simon Sturtevant.

definition: (philosophy) the doctrine that knowledge is acquired primarily by intuition.
The folding in of an outer layer so as to form a pocket in the surface.
etymology: Borrowed from French intussusception, or directly from Latin intussusceptiō, from intus (“within”) + susceptiō (“susception”).

definition: Influence or urge by gentle urging, caressing, or flattering.
example: He inveigled an introduction to my sister from me.
etymology: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman enveugler, alteration of aveugler (“to blind, to delude”), from Old French avogle (“without eyes”), from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”).

definition: In an inventive manner.
example: Picasso's liberated shapes and excitingly applied and inventively combined colours.

definition: Making an itemized list of merchandise or supplies on hand.
example: An inventory may be necessary to see if anything is missing.

definition: The inverse function of the cotangent; the angle that has a cotangent equal to a given number.
Spite and resentment at seeing the success of another (personified as one of the deadly sins).
Someone who watches examination candidates to prevent cheating.
etymology: From invigilate + -or, from Latin invigilatus, past participle of invigilo.

definition: Quality of being active or spirited or alive and vigorous.
The choicest or most essential or most vital part of some idea or experience.
example: The inwardness of conduct.
etymology: From Middle English inwardnesse; analysable as inward + -ness.

definition: An unsupported dogmatic assertion.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”), calque of Ancient Greek αὐτὸς ἔφα (autòs épha).

definition: The merchandise that is sold in an ironmonger's shop.
A person who makes articles of iron.
Incapable of being recovered or regained.
example: Irrecoverable data.
etymology: From Middle English irrecoverable, from Middle French irrecovrable. Attested earlier than recoverable. By surface analysis, ir- + recoverable.

definition: The doctrine that irredenta should be controlled by the country to which they are ethnically or historically related.
An advocate of irredentism.
Impossible to remedy or correct or redress.
example: An irremediable error.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin irremediābilis. By surface analysis, ir- + remediable.

definition: Without respect.
example: The student irreverently mimicked the teacher in his presence.

definition: The quality of being irreversible (once done it cannot be changed).
A sudden violent entrance; a bursting in.
example: The recent irruption of bad manners.
etymology: From Middle French irruption, from Latin irruptiō(n).

definition: Local anemia in a given body part sometimes resulting from vasoconstriction or thrombosis or embolism.

Any of various minerals consisting of hydrous silicates of aluminum or potassium etc. that crystallize in forms that allow perfect cleavage into very thin leaves; used as dielectrics because of their resistance to electricity.
example: The dashboard's genuine leather, / With isinglass curtains y' can roll right down, / In case there's a change in the weather.
etymology: Apparently from obsolete Dutch huisenblas, from German Hausenblase, from Hausen (“sturgeon of the Huso genus”) + Blase (“bladder”), with alteration after glass.

definition: (meteorology)an isogram connecting points having equal barometric pressure at a given time.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + βάρος (báros, “weight”), equivalent to iso- + bar-.

definition: A colorless pungent liquid sometimes used as a stimulant drug by drug abusers.
Equal in duration or interval.
example: The oscillations were isochronal.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + -ous.

definition: A widely used inhalation anesthetic.
The growth rates in different parts of a growing organism are the same.
example: Isometry is to metric spaces what isomorphism is to groups.
etymology: From New Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek ἰσομετρία (isometría), from ἰσο- (iso-) + -μετρία (-metría), from ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) and μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ια (-ia, “-y”). Equivalent to iso- + -metry.

definition: Drug (trade name Isordil) used to treat angina pectoris and congestive heart failure.
(physics) the property of being isotropic; having the same value when measured in different directions.
Print in italics.
Being nine more than thirty.
Large mostly white Australian stork.
etymology: From a Tupian term such as Old Tupi îabyru, said to mean either "swollen neck" or "one that spits".

definition: (19th century) a man's high tasseled boot.
example: That country has been under the jackboot of the military for years.
etymology: From Old French jaque (“coat of mail”).

definition: Meat cut from the thigh of a hog (usually smoked).
A loyal supporter.
example: Every politician has a following of janissaries.
etymology: ] Etymology tree Proto-Turkic *yaŋï Old Anatolian Turkish یكی (yäŋi) Ottoman Turkish یكی (yeñi) Proto-Turkic *čerig Old Anatolian Turkish چری (čäri) Ottoman Turkish چری (çeri) Ottoman Turkish یكیچری (yeñiçeri)bor.

definition: In a manner that jars and irritates.
example: The piano was jarringly out of tune.

definition: In a jaunty fashionable manner.
example: His hat sat jauntily on his full brown hair.

definition: Dark grey peccary with an indistinct white collar; of semi desert areas of Mexico and southwestern United States.
etymology: From Spanish javalina, jabalina, feminine form of jabalí (“wild boar”), from Andalusian Arabic جَبَلِي (jabalī) (in خِنْزِير جَبَلِيّ (ḵinzīr jabaliyy, “mountain pig”)), from Arabic جَبَل (jabal, “mountain”).

definition: Of animals having no jaw.
example: Jawless fishes, such as lampreys, often have large and sharp teeth.

definition: Eel-shaped vertebrate without jaws or paired appendages including the cyclostomes and some extinct forms.
Eel-shaped vertebrate without jaws or paired appendages including the cyclostomes and some extinct forms.
Cross the road at a red light.
etymology: Back-formation from jaywalker. Analyzable as jay (“a stupid person”) + walk.

definition: A reckless pedestrian who crosses a street illegally.
etymology: From jay (“a stupid person”) + walker; jay walker (“a pedestrian who doesn't pay attention to the road, endangering themselves and obstructing horses, carts, and automobiles”). First use appears c.

definition: A male musician who plays or composes jazz music.
A holy struggle or striving by a Muslim for a moral or spiritual or political goal.
Of insufficient quantity to meet a need.
example: The jejune diets of the very poor.

definition: The part of the small intestine between the duodenum and the ileum.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin iēiūnum, neuter of iēiūnus.

definition: Female donkey.
etymology: From Late Middle English genet, from Old French genet, from Old Catalan genet or Old Spanish ginete (“small fast horse;

definition: Mouselike jumping rodent.
etymology: From Arabic جَرْبُوع (jarbūʕ) or يَرْبُوع (yarbūʕ). Doublet of gerbil.

definition: Brush-tailed rat kangaroo.
Large Australian rat with hind legs adapted for leaping.
A long and mournful complaint.
example: A jeremiad against any form of government.
etymology: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, from Latin Ieremias, from Hebrew ירמיה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”). Named after biblical prophet Jeremiah, who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.

definition: A woman who jilts a lover.
etymology: Contraction of jillet (“a giddy girl, a jill-flirt”).

definition: Intensely poisonous tall coarse annual tropical weed having rank-smelling foliage, large white or violet trumpet-shaped flowers and prickly fruits.
(Islam) an invisible spirit mentioned in the Koran and believed by Muslims to inhabit the earth and influence mankind by appearing in the form of humans or animals.
(law) an estate secured to a prospective wife as a marriage settlement in lieu of a dower.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English joynture, from Old French jointure, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of juncture.

definition: Widely cultivated ornamental plant native to southern Europe but naturalized elsewhere having fragrant yellow or white clustered flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from French jonquille, itself a borrowing from Spanish junquillo. Possible doublet of junket.

definition: A Chinese rice gruel eaten for breakfast.
etymology: Unknown. Compare duck (“to lower the head or body”) or jink (“to make an evasive turn”). Attested since the 16th century.

definition: A small roadside establishment in the southeastern United States where you can eat and drink and dance to music provided by a jukebox.
A small roadside establishment in the southeastern United States where you can eat and drink and dance to music provided by a jukebox.
A small notebook for rough notes.
By journalists.
example: He is being journalistically crucified in his own country.

definition: Feeling jolly and jovial and full of good humor.
The emotion of great happiness.
In a joyous manner.
Celebrate a jubilee.
etymology: Either a back-formation from jubilation, or borrowed from Latin iūbilātus, perfect passive participle of iubilō (“to shout for joy”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Shake or vibrate rapidly and intensively.
example: The old engine was juddering.

definition: The arch of bone beneath the eye that forms the prominence of the cheek.
The craniometric point at the union of the frontal and temporal processes of the zygomatic bone.
A juicy appetizingness.
Formerly a high judicial officer.
etymology: From Late Latin justitiarius and justiciarius (“justiciar, judge, justice [of the peace]; judiciary, related to justice”), from Latin iūstitia (“justice”) + -āria (“-ary”).

definition: Conformity with some esthetic standard of correctness or propriety.
example: It was performed with justness and beauty.

definition: An esoteric or occult matter resembling the Kabbalah that is traditionally secret.
Any plant of the genus Kalmia.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Kalmia, from Swedish Kalm + translingual -ia, equivalent to Kalm + -ia.

definition: Antibiotic (trade name Kantrex) used to treat severe infections.
etymology: From (Streptomyces) kana(myceticus) + -mycin (“antibiotic produced from a Streptomyces strain”). The term kanamyceticus may comes from From Japanese 金 (kana-, “metal, money”) + Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs) + Latin -icus.

definition: Brush-tailed rat kangaroo.
A plant fiber from the kapok tree; used for stuffing and insulation.
etymology: Borrowed from Malay kapuk (“silky fibre from the silk-cotton tree; Ceiba pentandra”).

definition: Of an air current or wind; moving downward or down a slope because of cooling especially at night.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek καταιβατός (kataibatós, “down-going, descending”), from κατα- (kata-, “down”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go”).

definition: A wind caused by the downward motion of cold air.
Large green long-horned grasshopper of North America; males produce shrill sounds by rubbing together special organs on the forewings.
etymology: Onomatopoeic, from the sound a common true katydid (Pterophylla camellifolia) makes by stridulating. * katydid song: (file)

definition: Disagreeable aftereffects from the use of drugs (especially alcohol).
etymology: Borrowed from German Katzenjammer (“hangover”, literally “the wailing of cats”); a determinative compound formed from Katze (“cat”) + -n- + Jammer (“wailing; lamentation”).

definition: Resin of the kauri trees of New Zealand; found usually as a fossil; also collected for making varnishes and linoleum.
A dish of rice and hard-boiled eggs and cooked flaked fish.
etymology: From Hindi खिचड़ी (khicṛī), from Sanskrit खिच्चा (khiccā). Compare khichdi.

definition: (of hair) neat and tidy.
example: A nicely kempt beard.
etymology: Partly from both of the following: * An adjective use of kempt, the past participle of kemb (“(obsolete except UK, dialectal) to comb”), from Middle English kemben (“to comb (oneself or someone, or something);

definition: Conventional metaphoric name for something, used especially in Old English and Old Norse poetry.
example: Put in a kenning of salt.
etymology: From Middle English kenning, kening (“instruction, teaching; experience, knowledge; sight, view”), from kennen (“to make known, point out, reveal; to direct, instruct, teach; to know, perceive”) + -ing.

definition: A cap with a flat circular top and a visor.
etymology: From French képi, from Switzerland German Käppi, diminutive of Kappe, from Middle High German kappe, from Old High German kappa, from Latin cappa. Akin to English cap.

definition: A skin disease characterized by dark wartlike patches in the body folds; can be benign or malignant.
The civil and religious leader of a Muslim state considered to be a representative of Allah on earth.
example: Many radical Muslims believe a Khalifah will unite all Islamic lands and people and subjugate the rest of the world.

definition: American plover of inland waters and fields having a distinctive cry.
American plover of inland waters and fields having a distinctive cry.
Small mostly marine warm-water carp-like schooling fishes; used as bait or aquarium fishes or in mosquito control.
etymology: From killie (“killifish”, perhaps from kill (“channel, creek”)) or kill, + fish.

definition: In a very humorous manner.
Friendliness evidence by a kindly and helpful disposition.
A cathode-ray tube in a television receiver; translates the received signal into a picture on a luminescent screen.
A female relative.
etymology: From Middle English kynneswomman; equivalent to kin + -s- + -woman.

definition: A ceremonial four-inch curved dagger that Sikh men and women are obliged to wear at all times.
etymology: Borrowed from Punjabi ਕਿਰਪਾਨ (kirpān), from Sanskrit कृपाण (kṛpāṇa, “sword, dagger, sacrificial knife”), from कल्पयति (kalpáyati, “he orders, apportions, cuts, trims”).

definition: A knapsack (usually for a soldier).
Small pearl-grey gull of northern regions; nests on cliffs and has a rudimentary hind toe.
etymology: Originally Scots, imitative of the bird's call.

definition: A badly assembled collection of parts hastily assembled to serve some particular purpose.
etymology: Perhaps from British military slang, possibly based on Scots word kludge or kludgie (“common toilet”), or perhaps from German klug (“clever”).

definition: An electron tube used to generate or amplify electromagnetic radiation in the microwave region by velocity modulation.
Someone who buys old buildings or ships and breaks them up to recover the materials in them.
etymology: From Old Norse hnak (“saddle”) (whence Icelandic hnakkur (“saddle”)).

definition: Strike sharply.

definition: (Yiddish) a baked or fried turnover filled with potato or meat or cheese; often eaten as a snack.
etymology: Borrowed from Yiddish קניש (knish), from Polish knysz and Ukrainian книш (knyš).

definition: Used of old persons or old trees; covered with knobs or knots.
example: A knobbed stick.

definition: A hole in a board where a knot came out.
Having knowledge of.
example: Their intelligence and general knowingness was impressive.

definition: Christian fellowship or communion with God or with fellow Christians; said in particular of the early Christian community.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κοινωνία (koinōnía, “community, communion”).

definition: A small hill rising up from the African veld.
etymology: From (South African) Dutch kopje, diminutive of kop (“head”).

definition: The basic unit of money in Slovakia.

definition: 100 kurus equal 1 lira in Turkey.

definition: Fermented beverage resembling beer but made from rye or barley.

definition: The basic unit of money in Myanmar.

definition: A camp defended by a circular formation of wagons.

definition: A liplike structure that bounds a bodily orifice (especially any of the four labiate folds of a woman's vulva).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin labium (“a lip”). Doublet of lip.

definition: Irregularly slashed and jagged as if torn.
example: Lacerate leaves.
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1425, the adjective in 1514;

definition: Any of two families of insects with gauzy wings (Chrysopidae and Hemerobiidae); larvae feed on insect pests such as aphids.

definition: Any of two families of insects with gauzy wings (Chrysopidae and Hemerobiidae); larvae feed on insect pests such as aphids.
Work consisting of (or resembling) lace fabric.
Showing sorrow.

definition: A decorative work made of wood and covered with lacquer and often inlaid with ivory or precious metals.
A small gift (especially one given by a merchant to a customer who makes a purchase).

definition: Beat with a cane.

definition: Chop cut from a lamb.
Softly bright or radiant.

definition: A person who makes laminates (especially plastic laminates).
A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that is very effective in combination with zidovudine in treating AIDS and HIV.
Component consisting of a side piece opposite the moldboard.
Caught in European waters; slenderer than American lobster.
The capacity to understand a broad range of topics.

definition: A medical instrument for examining the larynx.
An East Indian sailor.

definition: In an enduring or permanent manner.
example: Only by good diplomacy will we lastingly establish peace.

The rig on a lateen-rigged sailing vessel.
Rigged with a triangular (lateen) sail.
Epicondyle near the lateral condyle of the femur.
A neural structure that serves as a processing station on the way from the retina to the occipital lobe of the cerebral cortex.
Localization of function on either the right or left sides of the brain.
Localization of function on either the right or left sides of the brain.
Derived from or imitative of Latin.
In an admirable manner.
A formulation added to laundry in order to stiffen the fabric.
A crystalline fatty acid occurring as glycerides in natural fats and oils (especially coconut oil and palm-kernel oil).
The quality possessed by something that is excessively expensive.
example: No one could question the lavishness of his parties; good taste was a different matter.
etymology: From lavish + -ness. Compare Dutch lafenis (“refreshment, lavishness”).

definition: The quality of being lax and neglectful.
example: There was a certain laxness in safety preparations that made the fire worse.

definition: Person who does no work.
Designated paved area beside a main road where cars can stop temporarily.
Small leaping insect that sucks the juices of plants.
The quality of being meager.

definition: Resembling or made to resemble leather; tough but pliable.
Work made of leather.
Man with strong sexual desires.
Tending toward the political left.
(law) an estate secured to a prospective wife as a marriage settlement in lieu of a dower.
Someone to whom a legacy is bequeathed.
An illusory feat; considered magical by naive observers.
A spear with three or more prongs; used for spearing fish (especially salmon).

definition: Mercifulness as a consequence of being lenient or tolerant.

definition: A man who takes photographs professionally.
Important pathogens causing Weil's disease or canicola fever.
etymology: From translingual Leptospira, from Ancient Greek λεπτός (leptós, “thin”) + σπεῖρα (speîra, “coil”).

definition: Chinese perennial with pyramidal racemes of white flowers and pungent aromatic roots used medicinally and as flavoring.
A part of the peritoneum attached to the stomach and liver and supporting the hepatic vessels.
Common scaup of North America; males have purplish heads.
Old World warbler similar to the greater whitethroat but smaller.
Man with strong sexual desires.

definition: An abnormal increase in the number of white blood cells in the blood as a result of infection (as in leukemia).
An abnormal lowering of the white blood cell count.
A muscle that serves to lift some body part (as the eyelid or lip).

definition: In a lewd and obscene manner.
etymology: From Middle English lewedly (“ignorantly, stupidly”); equivalent to lewd + -ly.

definition: Of or relating to lexicography.
Of or relating to lexicography.
Become more liberal.

definition: Belonging to the libido.
example: Libidinal impulses.

definition: (psychoanalysis) psychic energy produced by the libido.
(astronomy) a real or apparent slow oscillation of a moon or satellite.

definition: The position of a lieutenant.
Make one's day-to-day activities more efficient.

definition: The principal work of your career.

definition: The cheerful feeling you have when nothing is troubling you.
Giving no light.
example: Lightless stars ‘visible’ only to radio antennae.
etymology: From Middle English lightles, from Old English lēohtlēas, from Proto-West Germanic *leuhtalaus; equivalent to light (noun) + -less (“lacking, without”).

definition: Woody tissue.
Hard greenish-brown wood of the lignum vitae tree and other trees of the genus Guaiacum.
The probability of a specified outcome.
etymology: From Middle English liklinesse, lyklinesse; equivalent to likely + -ness.

definition: A border or edge of any of various body parts distinguished by color or structure.
etymology: From Middle English limbus, from Latin limbus (“edge, border”).

definition: Sweetened beverage of lime juice and water.
A widely occurring iron oxide ore; a mixture of goethite and hematite and lepidocrocite.
A colorless fragrant liquid found in many essential oils.
A characteristic property that defines the apparent individual nature of something.

definition: A print that is made from a design carved in relief into a block of linoleum.
Extraordinarily courageous.
Assign great social importance to.

Sarcoma of fat cells.
An artificially made microscopic vesicle into which nucleic acids can be packaged; used in molecular biology as a transducing vector.
etymology: From lipo- (“fat”) + -some (“body”). From Ancient Greek λίπος (lípos, “fat”) and Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “soma”).

definition: An ACE inhibiting drug (trade names Prinivil or Zestril) administered as an antihypertensive and after heart attacks.
All the listeners collectively of a particular radio programme, station, or broadcaster.
example: In 2012, the share of radio listenership on mobile phones has increased by 10%, as compared to 2009.
etymology: From listener + -ship (suffix denoting a property or state of being).

definition: A feeling of lack of interest or energy.
A printmaker who uses lithography.
Any plant of the genus Lithops native to Africa having solitary yellow or white flowers and thick leaves that resemble stones.
etymology: From the genus name, translingual Lithops.

definition: (of time) constituting the full extent or duration.
example: All the livelong day.
etymology: From Middle English live long, leve-long, lefe long (as in Alle the lefe longe daye), equivalent to lief + long.

definition: The property of being animated; having animal life as distinguished from plant life.
A word borrowed from another language; e.g. ‘blitz’ is a German word borrowed into modern English.
example: "Calque" is a loanword with French origins, and "loanword" is a calque with German origins.
etymology: A calque of German Lehnwort, equivalent to loan + word. Compare West Frisian lienwurd, Dutch leenwoord, Danish låneord, Swedish lånord, Icelandic lánsorð.

definition: Of or relating to or affecting a lobe.
example: Lobar pneumonia.

Having or resembling a lobe or lobes.

definition: A bird's foot having separate toes each with membranous flaps along the sides.
Surgical removal of a lobe from any organ of the body (as the lung or brain).

A small lobe or subdivision of a lobe.
Advocating or supporting the interests of a particular locality.

Castling on the queenside.

definition: A type of ship invented and used by the Vikings for trade, commerce, exploration, and warfare during the Viking Age.
example: The longships had two methods of propulsion: oars and sail.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English *langschip, from Old English langsċip (“a longship, a large warship”), equivalent to long + ship.

definition: The common American weasel distinguished by large size and black-tipped tail.
Being or having leaves that can be easily removed or rearranged.
example: Loose-leaf paper.
etymology: From loose + leaf (“sheet of a book, magazine, etc.”).

definition: Any of numerous herbs and subshrubs of the genus Lythrum.
etymology: Calque of Ancient Greek λυσιμάχειον (lusimákheion), as if from λύσις (lúsis, “loosening”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle, strife”).

definition: Herbs and shrubs and small trees with pink or purple flowers.
Evergreen tree of warm regions having fuzzy yellow olive-sized fruit with a large free stone; native to China and Japan.

definition: Evergreen tree of warm regions having fuzzy yellow olive-sized fruit with a large free stone; native to China and Japan.
An abnormal inward (forward) curvature of the vertebral column.

definition: A hard protective sheath (as secreted by certain protoctists, for example).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lōrīca, literally "a corselet of thongs", probably from lorum (“thong”).

definition: A substance capable of reducing friction by making surfaces smooth or slippery.
Feeling morbid sexual desire or a propensity to lewdness.

definition: Pigment occurring in luminescent organisms (as fireflies); emits heatless light when undergoing oxidation.
Relating to play or playfulness.

A nerve plexus formed by the ventral divisions of the coccygeal and sacral and lumbar nerves; supplies the lower limbs and perineum and coccygeal area.
Resembling the new moon in shape.
example: A lunate beak.
etymology: First attested in 1777; borrowed from Latin lūnātus (“crescent-shaped”), from lūna (“moon”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: One of the eight small wrist bones.
Temporary fortification like a detached bastion.

definition: Someone who moves forward suddenly (as in fencing).
Air-breathing fish having an elongated body and fleshy paired fins; certain species construct mucus-lined mud coverings in which to survive drought.
The property of being lush and abundant and a pleasure to the senses.

definition: In a lustful manner.

definition: Dried cod soaked in a lye solution before boiling to give it a gelatinous consistency.

Being eight more than fifty.
Being three more than sixty.

etymology: From Latin lycanthrōpus, from Ancient Greek λυκάνθρωπος (lukánthrōpos) – a compound of λύκος (lúkos, “wolf”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, human”). By surface analysis, lyc- + -anthrope.

definition: Cooked with onions.
example: For dinner, we had beef with potatoes lyonnaise.
etymology: From French lyonnaise (“in the manner of Lyon”).

definition: A neurotropic non-arbovirus of the family Rhabdoviridae that causes rabies.
Separate into constituents by soaking.
etymology: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin mācerātus, perfect passive participle of mācerō (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from Proto-Indo-European *mag-, *mak- (“to knead”), whence make. Cognate with French macérer.

definition: A crafty and involved plot to achieve your (usually sinister) ends.
etymology: From Middle English machynacion, machynacyon, from Middle French machination and directly Latin māchinātiōnem, from māchinor (“devise, invent”). By surface analysis, machinate + -ion or machine + -ation.

definition: Evolution on a large scale extending over geologic era and resulting in the formation of new taxonomic groups.
Any very large complex molecule; found only in plants and animals.
Without using a microscope.

Muslim schools in Bangladesh and Pakistan.

In a magnanimous manner.

Mexican plant used especially for making pulque which is the source of the colorless Mexican liquor, mescal.

Not adroit.

Empty rhetoric or insincere or exaggerated talk.
A salt or ester of maleic acid; used as a nontricyclic antidepressant drug for psychomotor activation.
The act of calling down a curse that invokes evil (and usually serves as an insult).
A colorless crystalline compound found in unripe fruit (such as apples or tomatoes or cherries) and used mainly to make polyester resins.

definition: In a malevolent manner.

definition: Feeling a need to see others suffer.

Grape used to make malmsey wine.

definition: The branch of zoology that studies mammals.
The capability of being managed or controlled.
In a manner that cannot be evaded.
Baboon of west Africa with a bright red and blue muzzle and blue hindquarters.

definition: An oxide of manganese found naturally as hausmannite.
Hard fiber used in making coarse twine; from Philippine agave plants.
Easily managed (controlled or taught or molded).
Socially correct in behavior.

definition: A pressure gauge for comparing pressures of a gas.
etymology: From French manomètre, formed from Ancient Greek μανός (manós, “thin, rare”) + μέτρον (métron), equivalent to mano- + -meter.

definition: Resembling or characteristic of a prophet or prophecy.
example: Mantic powers.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μαντικός (mantikós), from μάντις (mántis, “seer, soothsayer”), from μαίνομαι (maínomai, “I am mad, raving”).

definition: Predacious long-bodied large-eyed insect of warm regions; rests with forelimbs raised as in prayer.
A woman's silk or lace scarf.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish mantilla (“large veil; small cape”), from manta (“blanket, cloth, cloth banner”) + -illa (diminutive).

definition: Shelf that projects from wall above fireplace.
The making of maps and charts.
Large African black-and-white carrion-eating stork; its downy underwing feathers are used to trim garments.
etymology: From French marabout, from Portuguese maraboto, marabuto, from Moroccan Arabic مْرَابِط (mrabeṭ) (standard Arabic مُرَابِط (murābiṭ, “soldier stationed in fortified outpost”)).

definition: A percussion instrument consisting of a hollow gourd containing pebbles or beans; often played in pairs.
etymology: From Brazilian Portuguese maraca, derived from Old Tupi maraká or Paraguayan Guarani mbaraka (“rattle”).

definition: Any of numerous herbs of the genus Maranta having tuberous starchy roots and large sheathing leaves.
Wildflower having vibrant deep pink tubular evening-blooming flowers; found in sandy and desert areas from southern California to southern Colorado and into Mexico.
Relegate to a lower or outer edge, as of specific groups of people.
example: We must not marginalize the poor in our society.

definition: The property of being marginal or on the fringes.
Organisms (plants and animals) that live specifically at or near the bottom of a sea.
A pointed iron hand tool that is used to separate strands of a rope or cable (as in splicing).
A solid solution of carbon in alpha-iron that is formed when steel is cooled so rapidly that the change from austenite to pearlite is suppressed; responsible for the hardness of quenched steel.
etymology: Named after German metallurgist Adolf Martens (1850–1914).

definition: The abnormal development of male sexual characteristics in a female (usually as the result of hormone therapies or adrenal malfunction).
A large muscle that raises the lower jaw and is used in chewing.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin massētēr. Compare French masséter.

definition: Having no lord or master.
example: Harsh punishments for sturdy vagabonds and masterless men.
etymology: From Middle English masterles, maisterles, equivalent to master + -less. Compare Dutch meesterloos (“masterless”), German meisterlos (“masterless”), Icelandic meistaralaus (“masterless”).

definition: Someone who arranges (or tries to arrange) marriages for others.
example: There are multiple sets of matchers for various types of searches.
etymology: From match + -er. Cognate with Old Frisian mekere (“matchmaker”).

definition: An early style of musket; a slow-burning wick would be lowered into a hole in the breech to ignite the charge.
A person who murders their mother.
example: Gerald was imprisoned for matricide: he strangled his mother.
etymology: From French matricide, from Latin mātricīda (“person who kills his own mother”) and mātricīdium (“the murder of one's mother”). By surface analysis, matri- + -cide.

definition: Brittle flat bread eaten at Passover.
A Jewish dumpling made of matzo meal; usually served in soup.
Meal made from ground matzos.
Someone who is dazzlingly skilled in any field.

The larva of beetles of the family Tenebrionidae.

definition: Scalelike plant-eating insect coated with a powdery waxy secretion; destructive especially of fruit trees.

definition: In a nasty ill-tempered manner.

etymology: From Middle English meneli, meneliche, equivalent to mean + -ly.

definition: Without limits in extent or size or quantity.
A person who makes measurements.
An anthelmintic used to treat hookworm and pinworm and roundworm infestations.
A philosopher who subscribes to the doctrine of mechanism.
In a mechanistic manner.
example: Handel achieves a huge breadth of musical thought when composing almost mechanistically in the least weighty of styles.

definition: Equip with armed and armored motor vehicles.
example: Mechanize armies.

definition: A neural structure that serves as the last of a series of processing centers along the auditory pathway from the cochlea to the temporal lobe of the cerebral cortex.
(medicine) something that treats or prevents or alleviates the symptoms of disease.
etymology: From Middle English medicament, either from Middle French médicament or its etymon, Latin medicāmentum.

definition: In a meditative manner.
example: Round and round, while meditatively, as a cow chewing the cud, he let his eyes rest on the flat water ahead of him.

definition: Small deciduous tree of southern Africa having edible fruit.
etymology: From Middle English medler, medeler, from Old French medler, meslier, from medle, mesdle (“medlar fruit”), from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon).

definition: Small deciduous Eurasian tree cultivated for its fruit that resemble crab apples.
A progestin compound (trade name Provera) used to treat menstrual disorders.
A white clayey mineral.
A large sum of money (especially as pay or profit).
example: They sank megabucks into their new house.

definition: Memorial consisting of a very large stone forming part of a prehistoric structure (especially in western Europe).
etymology: PIE word *méǵh₂s From mega- (prefix meaning ‘very large, great’) + -lith (suffix meaning ‘stone’), a back-formation from megalithic probably modelled after monolith. from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”)

definition: (Yiddish) a long boring tediously detailed account.
example: He insisted on giving us the whole megillah.
etymology: From Hebrew מגילה / מְגִלָּה (m'gilá, “scroll”). Doublet of magilla.

definition: A cell in the basal layer of the epidermis that produces melanin under the control of the melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
A tan discoloration of a woman's face that is associated with pregnancy or with the use of oral contraceptives.
etymology: From Latin melasma, from Ancient Greek μέλασμα (mélasma), from μελαίνειν (melaínein, “to blacken”) + -σμα (-sma), from μέλας (mélas, “black”).

definition: Abnormally dark tarry feces containing blood (usually from gastrointestinal bleeding).
etymology: From New Latin melaena, based on Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”).

definition: As in a melodrama.
example: Here, the hero is melodramatically reunited with the heroine.

definition: Antineoplastic drug (trade name Alkeran) used to treat multiple myeloma and some other malignancies.
A theory of mental content based on an analogy with Darwinian evolution.
The quality of being worth remembering.
example: Continuous change results in lack of memorability.
