definition: A water wheel with buckets attached to the rim; used to raise water for transfer to an irrigation channel.
etymology: From Spanish noria, from Arabic نَاعُورَة (nāʕūra), from Classical Syriac ܢܥܘܪܬܐ (nāʿōrtāʾ, “water wheel; growler”), from ܢܥܪ (nʿar, “to roar, growl, bray”).

definition: A favorite game bird of eastern and central United States.
Breeds in Arctic regions of Old and New Worlds; large flocks often seen far out at sea.
A tricyclic antidepressant drug (trade name Pamelor) used along with psychotherapy to treat dysthymic depression; may interact dangerously if taken with other drugs.
Put into notation, as of music or choreography.
example: Nowadays, you can notate an entire ballet; in the old days, the steps had to be memorized.
etymology: First attested in 1871; back-formation from notation or from Latin notātus, perfect passive participle of notō; either way, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, note + -ate.

definition: A flexible rodlike structure that forms the supporting axis of the body in the lowest chordates and lowest vertebrates and in embryos of higher vertebrates.
Converting something into the form of a novel.
A small nub (especially an undeveloped fruit or ear of corn).
example: As an avid button collector, I have had to develop an efficient way of removing the nubbin of thread from the buttonhole.

definition: Of textiles; having a rough surface.
Having a nucleus or occurring in the nucleus.
example: Nucleated cells.

definition: Any of various marine gastropods of the suborder Nudibranchia having a shell-less and often beautifully colored body.
etymology: Circa 19th century, borrowed from translingual Nudibranchia, from Latin nudus (“naked”) + branchia (“gills”).

definition: A plate mounted on the front and back of car and bearing the car's registration number.
A spirit believed to inhabit an object or preside over a place (especially in ancient Roman religion).
Determine the number or amount of.
etymology: From Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). By surface analysis, Latin numerus + -ate.

definition: Naming numbers.
etymology: From Middle English numeracioun, from Latin numerātiō. By surface analysis, numerate + -ion.

definition: Any notation for the representation of numbers.
Of or relating to numerology.
A collector and student of money (and coins in particular).
Uncontrolled nodding.
etymology: 1610s, from Latin nūtātiō (“nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”). Compare mutation.

definition: A source of materials to nourish the body.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English nutriment, from Latin nūtrīmentum.

definition: Spiral-horned South African antelope with a fringe of white hairs along back and neck.
etymology: Probably borrowed from Tsonga nyala. The alternative form inyala is from Zulu inyala.

definition: Abnormally intense sexual desire in women.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin, from Latin nympha + -mania. By surface analysis, nympho- + mania.

definition: An antifungal and antibiotic (trade names Mycostatin and Nystan) discovered in New York State; derived from soil fungi actinomycetes.
Ill-mannered and coarse and contemptible in behavior or appearance.
example: Her stupid oafish husband.

definition: Loose hemp or jute fiber obtained by unravelling old ropes; when impregnated with tar it was used to caulk seams and pack joints in wooden ships.
A male who rows a boat.
A kiln for drying hops.
etymology: From Middle English ost, from Old English āst (“a kiln”), from Proto-Germanic *aistaz (“kiln”), from *aisǭ (“fire”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to burn; fire”).

definition: A building containing an oast (a kiln for drying hops); usually has a conical or pyramidal roof.
Of or related to or derived from oats.
example: Oaten bread.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English oten, *aten (“oaten”); equivalent to oat + -en. Cognate with Scots aiten (“oaten”).

definition: A persistent but subordinate motif.
etymology: From Italian obbligato. Piecewise doublet of obliged.

definition: An incidental remark.
etymology: From Latin obiter dictum (“something said by the way”).

definition: (of a leaf shape) having a broad rounded apex and a tapering base.
A leaf having a rounded apex and tapering base.
In an obligatory manner.
example: This rule applies obligatorily.

definition: A musician who plays the oboe.
A policy of opposition to enlightenment or the spread of knowledge.
etymology: From Latin obscūrans, from obscūrō (“to cover, darken, obscure”) + -ism.

definition: A person who is deliberately vague.
Extreme compulsiveness.
example: His obsessiveness makes it hard to get a word in when you talk to him.

definition: Noisily and stubbornly defiant.
example: Obstreperous boys.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin obstreperus, first attested circa 17th c. Compare obstropulous.

definition: The quality of being slow to understand.
Back part of the head or skull.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin occiput (“the back part of the head”). Compare sinciput.

definition: An eye having a single lens.
etymology: From Latin ocellus (“little eye”), from oculus (“eye”).

definition: Desert shrub of southwestern United States and Mexico having slender naked spiny branches that after the rainy season put forth foliage and clusters of red flowers.
etymology: From American Spanish ocotillo, from ocote.

definition: A measuring instrument for measuring angles to a celestial body; similar to a sextant but with 45 degree calibration.
etymology: From Latin octāns. Doublet of Octans.

definition: A person skilled in testing for defects of vision in order to prescribe corrective glasses.
etymology: From French oculiste (“oculist”), from Latin oculus (“eye”).

definition: A woman slave in a harem.
etymology: Borrowed from French odalisque, from Ottoman Turkish اوطهلق (odalık, “chambermaid”), from اوده (oda, “room”).

definition: Somewhat strange.
The branch of medicine dealing with the anatomy and development and diseases of the teeth.
Applies to nonhuman mammals: a state or period of heightened sexual arousal and activity.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin oestrus (“gadfly, sting, frenzy”), from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eys-, used to form words denoting passion;

definition: More often or more frequently.
Many times at short intervals.
Front consisting of the conical head of a missile or rocket that protects the payload from heat during its passage through the atmosphere.
etymology: From late Middle English ogif, egeve, egeove, from Old French ogive, œgive, augive. Doublet of ogee.

definition: Cloth treated on one side with a drying oil or synthetic resin.
Consisting of or covered with oil.
Primly fastidious.
Attractively old-fashioned (but not necessarily authentic).
example: Down this street is a lovely olde worlde bookshop.

definition: Somewhat elderly.
An experienced person who has been through many battles; someone who has given long service.
Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech.
example: Oleaginous hypocrisy.
etymology: Borrowed from French oléagineux, borrowed from Medieval Latin oleāginōsus (“oily”), from olea (“the olive tree or its fruit”).

definition: Process of the ulna that forms the outer bump of the elbow and fits into the fossa of the humerus when the arm is extended.
Process of the ulna that forms the outer bump of the elbow and fits into the fossa of the humerus when the arm is extended.
A naturally occurring mixture of a resin and an essential oil; obtained from certain plants.
A cell of the oligodendroglia.
A government appointee who investigates complaints by private persons against the government.
A fold of peritoneum supporting the viscera.
A code of silence practiced by the Mafia; a refusal to give evidence to the police about criminal activities.

Infestation with slender threadlike roundworms (filaria) deposited under the skin by the bite of black fleas; when the eyes are involved it can result in blindness; common in Africa and tropical America.
etymology: From New Latin Onchocerca (a genus of parasitic worms), from Ancient Greek ὄγκος (ónkos, “barb”) + κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”) + -iasis.

definition: Of or relating to or practicing oncology.
example: Oncological nurse.

definition: One part in a trillion equal parts.
Of or relating to or characterized by onomatopoeia.
(military) an offensive against an enemy (using weapons).
etymology: From on- + rush. Compare Middle English onresen (“to rush upon; attack”), from Old English onrǣsan (“to rush, rush on”); Old English onrǣs (“an onrush, assault, attack”).

definition: The visual property of something having a milky brightness and a play of colors from the surface.
Having a play of lustrous rainbow colors.
example: A milky opalescent (or opaline) luster.

definition: Incomprehensibility resulting from obscurity of meaning.
A woodworking plane designed to cut rabbets.
Limbless scaly elongate reptile; some are venomous.
etymology: From Latin ophidia (from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “snake”)) + -ian.

definition: Medical instrument for examining the retina of the eye.
Someone who offers opposition.
Retinal protein formed by the action of light on rhodopsin.
etymology: Shortened form of rhodopsin. From Ancient Greek ὄψις (ópsis, “sight”) + -in.

definition: Indicating an option or wish.
etymology: From Middle French optatif, from Late Latin optātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική (euktikḗ, “related to wishing”), from Latin optātus, past participle of optāre.

definition: A mood (as in Greek or Sanskrit) that expresses a wish or hope; expressed in English by modal verbs.
The crossing of the optic nerves from the two eyes at the base of the brain.
Quality or state in which choice or discretion is allowed.
example: The usual optionality of these tasks entails the risk of students not fulfilling them in an effective way.

definition: A superior grade of black tea; grown in India and Sri Lanka and Java.
Of the color between red and yellow; similar to the color of a ripe orange.
example: That coat that you're wearing looks almost orangish in the evening sun.

definition: Of red tinged with orange.
Surgical removal of one or both testicles.
Of or relating to or belonging to an organism (considered as a whole).
example: The organismic theory of the state.

definition: A system of principles for philosophic or scientific investigations; an instrument for acquiring knowledge.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon). Doublet of organ, organum, and orgue.

definition: Reverent petition to a deity.
example: 1917, Wilfred Owen, Anthem for Doomed Youth Only the stuttering rifles' rapid rattle Can patter out their hasty orisons.
etymology: From Middle English orisoun, from Anglo-Norman oreison, oresoun etc. and Old French oraisun etc., from Latin ōrātiō, ōrātiōnem (“discourse, prayer”) (whence also English oration).

definition: Brass that looks like gold; used to decorate furniture.
Cavity formed by the pharynx at the back of the mouth.
A special shoe insole used to provide better support for feet, thus alleviating pain.
Brownish Old World bunting often eaten as a delicacy.
etymology: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

definition: Brownish Old World bunting often eaten as a delicacy.
The large cranial bone forming the front part of the cranium: includes the upper part of the orbits.
Flexible twig of a willow tree.
etymology: Borrowed from French osier (“basket willow, withy”)

definition: By means of osmosis.
Inflammation of a bone as a consequence of infection or trauma or degeneration.
A cell from which bone develops.
Cell that functions in the breakdown and resorption of bone tissue.
Abnormal softening of bones caused by deficiencies of phosphorus or calcium or vitamin D.
Tiny marine and freshwater crustaceans with a shrimp-like body enclosed in a bivalve shell.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὀστρακώδης (ostrakṓdēs, “covered with shell”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot; shell”); compare translingual Ostracoda.

definition: Inflammation of the external ear (including auricle and ear canal).
A specialist in the disorders of the ear or nose or throat.
The branch of medicine concerned with the ear.
The medical specialty that deals with diseases of the ear, nose and throat.
A dungeon with the only entrance or exit being a trap door in the ceiling.
etymology: Borrowed from French oubliette, from oublier (“to forget”).

definition: A voluminous garment worn over the inner cassock by bishops, priests, deacons, and monastics as their regular outer wear.
Outdo someone in trickery.
In an outlandish manner.
example: The Bavarian was outlandishly dressed in lederhosen.

definition: Illegality as a consequence of unlawful acts; defiance of the law.
Defeat by more skillful maneuvering.
example: The English troops outmaneuvered the Germans.

definition: Situated at the farthest possible point from a center.
Excessive excess.
A part of the city far removed from the center.
example: They built a factory on the outskirts of the city.

definition: The outer sole of a shoe or boot that is the bottom of the shoe and makes contact with the ground.
In an outspoken manner.
example: He was outspokenly critical of the Government's new social policy.

definition: Fully extended in width.
example: Outspread wings.
etymology: From Middle English outspreden, equivalent to out- + spread. Cognate with Dutch uitspreiden (“to outspread, stretch, unfold”), Danish udsprede (“to outspread”), Swedish utspridda (“to outspread”).

definition: What is produced in a given time period.
Defeat by a majority of votes.
example: The Democrats outvoted the Republicans.

definition: Excessive activity.
example: Overactivity of the sebaceous glands causes the skin to become oily.

definition: Excessively ambitious.
Unnecessarily cautious.
example: Sometimes it doesn't pay to be overcautious in business.

definition: Someone who overcomes and establishes ascendancy and control by force or persuasion.
example: An overcomer of pain.
etymology: From Middle English overcomere, equivalent to overcome + -er.

definition: (psychiatry) an attempt to overcome a real or imagined defect or unwanted trait by overly exaggerating its opposite.
Cause to crowd together too much.
example: The students overcrowded the cafeteria.

definition: Draw more money from than is available.
example: She overdrew her account.

definition: Excessively or abnormally emotional.
Place special or excessive emphasis on.
example: I cannot overemphasize the importance of this book.

definition: Unduly enthusiastic.
Excessive exertion; so much exertion that discomfort or injury results.
Exploitation to the point of diminishing returns.
example: The overexploitation of forests left the island nearly denuded of trees.
etymology: By surface analysis, over- + exploitation, or, by surface analysis, overexploit + -ation.

definition: Strain excessively.
example: He overextended himself when he accepted the additional assignment.

definition: Feed excessively.
Fly over.
example: The small size of the airstrip meant that pilots would frequently overfly and have to circle back.

definition: Exceeding demand.
etymology: From Middle English overful, overfulle, from Old English oferfull (“overfull”), from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *uberfullaz; equivalent to over- + full.

definition: On or to the other side of a page.
example: Data tabulated overleaf.

definition: Lie upon; lie on top of.
example: The granite overlies the older rocks.
etymology: From Middle English overlien, overliggen, equivalent to over- + lie (“to be reclined”). Compare West Frisian oerlizze, German überliegen, Danish overligge, Swedish överligga, Norwegian overligge.

definition: Very great in quantity; overabundant.
example: Showed overmuch affection.
etymology: From Middle English overmuche, overmuchel, from Old English ofermiċel, ofermyċel (“overmuch, excessive”), equivalent to over- + much. Compare overmany and overmore. Doublet of overmickle.

definition: A guest who stays overnight.
Produce in excess; produce more than needed or wanted.
A calculation that results in an estimate that is too high.
Spread across or over.
etymology: From Middle English overspreden, from Old English ofersprǣdan; equivalent to over- + spread. Cognate with Dutch overspreiden (“to overspread”), German überspreiten (“to overspread”).

definition: Strain abnormally.
etymology: From Middle English overstrecchen, corresponding to over- + stretch. Compare Dutch overstrekken (“to overstretch”), German überstrecken (“to overstretch”).

definition: Of or pertaining to or of the nature of or characteristic of a sheep or sheep.
etymology: The adjective is borrowed from Late Latin ovīnus (“ovine”) + English -ine (suffix with the sense ‘of or relating to’ forming adjectives).

definition: Egg-laying.
example: The echidna is a monotreme, which is the extremely small subset of oviparous mammals.
etymology: Adapted borrowing of Late Latin ōviparus + -ous. By surface analysis, ovi- + -parous.

definition: Any plant or flower of the genus Oxalis.
A salt or ester of oxalacetic acid.
A cart that is drawn by an ox.
Add oxygen to or combine with oxygen.
The process of oxidizing; the addition of oxygen to a compound with a loss of electrons; always occurs accompanied by reduction.
An enzyme that catalyzes oxidation-reduction.
Any compound containing the group -C=NOH.
etymology: From German Oxim, from oxy- + Imid. From Oxy + -ime (from clipping of imide).

definition: An oxidoreductase that catalyzes the incorporation of molecular oxygen.
etymology: From German Oxygenase, corresponding to oxygen + -ase.

definition: Edible agaric with a soft greyish cap growing in shelving masses on dead wood.
Black-and-white shorebird with stout legs and bill; feed on oysters etc.
Worthless or oversimplified ideas.
Opposed to war.
example: Even the most pacifistic nations still maintain an armed police force.

definition: A workhorse used as a pack animal.
etymology: From pack + horse, possibly (from an uncertain date) via Middle English palhors (read pakhorse).

definition: A man who travels about selling his wares (as on the streets or at carnivals).
A collector of miscellaneous useless objects.
A large wheel fitted with paddles and driven by an engine in order to propel a boat.
An owner or proprietor of an inn in Italy.
etymology: From Italian padrone, from Latin patronus. Doublet of patron, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

definition: A boy who is employed to run errands.
Lending itself to being painted.
example: A highly paintable landscape.

definition: A box containing a collection of cubes or tubes of artists' paint.
The branch of ecology that studies ancient ecology.
East Indian tree bearing a profusion of intense vermilion velvet-textured blooms and yielding a yellow dye.
A branch of paleontology that deals with the origin and growth and structure of fossil animals and plants as living organisms.
The branch of ecology that studies ancient ecology.
The study of ancient forms of writing (and the deciphering of them).
etymology: From paleo- + -graphy; imitating Latin palaeographia for the first sense and French paléographie and paléogéographie for the second and third senses.

definition: A public place in ancient Greece or Rome devoted to the training of wrestlers and other athletes.
Easing the severity of a pain or a disease without removing the cause.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French palliation, from Latin palliare (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin pallium (“cloak”). By surface analysis, palliate + -ion.

definition: (of the feet of water birds) having three toes connected by a thin fold of skin.
example: Although palmate leaves are typical of most Western maples, a number of species have leaves without lobes.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin palmātus (“hand-shaped, palm-leaf shaped”), from palma (“palm, palm-tree”). Equivalent to palm + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French palmé.

definition: A leaf resembling an open hand; having lobes radiating from a common point.
In a palmate manner.
example: Palmately cleft.

definition: Having lobes radiating from a central point.
Very lively and profitable.
example: A palmy time for stockbrokers.

definition: A second-rate prize fighter.
etymology: Used in the US since the 1920s, originally primarily of boxers. Popularized by Jack Conway of Variety, who also popularized baloney and bimbo.

definition: Examine (a body part) by palpation.
example: The nurse palpated the patient's stomach.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin palpātus, perfect passive participle of palpō (“touch softly”).

definition: Photographic film sensitive to light of all colors (including red).
Any of numerous small food fishes; especially those caught with hook and line and not available on the market.
example: Panfish are caught primarily for eating, rather than for sport.

definition: A beggar who approaches strangers asking for money.
etymology: Obscure. Speculative. Panhandling always seems to involve a container for receiving loose change, so perhaps the term refers to a small handled pan, or to the container as the pan and the arm(s) holding it as the handle.

definition: The hypothesis that microorganisms may transmit life from outer space to habitable bodies; or the process of such transmission.
Trousers worn in former times.
etymology: Borrowed from French pantalon, from Italian Pantalone (a character in Commedia dell'arte), from Spanish Pantaleon (surname).

definition: Short underpants for women or children.
A vitamin of the vitamin B complex that performs an important role in the oxidation of fats and carbohydrates and certain amino acids; occurs in many foods.
A proteolytic enzyme obtained from the unripe papaya; used as a meat tenderizer.
etymology: Attested since the late 1800s. From papaya + -in.

definition: Small tree native to the eastern United States having oblong leaves and fleshy fruit.
etymology: Via Portuguese and Spanish papaya from Lokono papáia; compare also Kari'na kapaja.

definition: Small tree native to the eastern United States having oblong leaves and fleshy fruit.
Absorbent paper used as toweling.
A surface having parabolic sections parallel to a single coordinate axis and elliptic sections perpendicular to that axis.
A concave reflector used to produce a parallel beam when the source is placed at its focus or to focus an incoming parallel beam.
A virus that causes upper respiratory infection (including the common cold and bronchiolitis); most often in children.
Adjacent to the nasal cavities.
example: Paranasal sinus.

definition: Any of the paired sinuses in the bones of the face adjacent to the nasal cavity that are lined with mucous membrane that is continuous with the lining of the nasal cavities.
Abnormal sexual activity.
A poisonous yellow solid used in solution as a herbicide.
Poisoning caused by ingestion of paraquat; characterized by progressive damage to the esophagus and liver and kidneys.
By parenteral means.
example: The drug is intended to be administered parenterally.

definition: In a parenthetical manner.
example: He added parenthetically that he would not attend the wedding ceremony.

definition: Having no parent or parents or not cared for by parent surrogates.
A manicurist who trims the fingernails.
Appreciably or disagreeably cold.
example: We went to a beautiful parky place over by the river.

definition: Someone who kills his or her parent.
etymology: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

definition: Someone who has or gives or receives a part or a share.
example: The joint was passed around the circle, but he was not a partaker, so he waved it away.

definition: (of reproduction) not involving the fusion of male and female gametes in reproduction.
example: Parthenogenetic forms.

definition: A focus on something particular.
(Romance languages) relating to or denoting a part of a whole or a quantity that is less than the whole.
example: A partitive construction.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English partitif, borrowed from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.

definition: Characteristic of someone who has risen economically or socially but lacks the social skills appropriate for this new position.
etymology: Borrowed from French parvenu, past participle of parvenir, from Latin perveniō (“arrive, reach”). See also parvenue f

definition: Large African antelope with long straight nearly upright horns.
Tall tufted perennial tropical American grass naturalized as pasture and forage grass in southern United States.
etymology: From translingual Paspalum (genus name), from Koine Greek πάσπαλος (páspalos, “type of millet”).

definition: Key that secures entrance everywhere.
Relating to or characteristic of the passeriform birds.
etymology: Adjective sense 1 is borrowed from New Latin Passer (“bird genus”) (from Latin passer (“sparrow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out;

definition: Any of various chiefly tropical American vines some bearing edible fruit.
etymology: Calque of Italian fior della Passione or Latin flōs Passiōnis; after the appearance and number of its various parts, thought to be symbolic of Christ's passion.

definition: Tropical woody tendril-climbing vines.
Any of various chiefly tropical American vines some bearing edible fruit.
Submission to others or to outside influences.
Key that secures entrance everywhere.
A workman who pastes.
The part between the fetlock and the hoof.
etymology: From Middle English pastron, pastroun, pasturne, from Old French pasturon, diminutive of pasture (“shackle for a horse in pasture”), alteration of Late Latin pastōria after the suffix -ure.

definition: Partial sterilization of foods at a temperature that destroys harmful microorganisms without major changes in the chemistry of the food.
etymology: From French pasteurisation, from the surname of its inventor, Louis Pasteur.

definition: Heat food in order to kill harmful microorganisms.
example: Pasteurize milk.
etymology: Borrowed from French pasteuriser. From Louis Pasteur, the inventor of the process, + -ize.

definition: A musical composition that evokes rural life.
example: She was in the country, painting her first pastorale.
etymology: From French, from Middle French pastorale; or from Italian pastorale, hence the plural pastorali.

definition: Reddish long-tailed monkey of west Africa.
Unevenness in quality or performance.
The openness (lack of obstruction) of a bodily passage or duct.
The male head of family or tribe.
etymology: (c. 1425 to 1475) From late Middle English paterfamilias, from Latin pater familiās. From Latin pater (“father”) + familiās, archaic genitive of familia (“family; household”).

definition: In a paternal manner.
example: He behaves very paternally toward his young bride.

definition: Someone on patrol duty; an individual or a member of a group that patrols an area.
Having a large belly.
example: He exercised every day to avoid becoming paunchy in his old age.

definition: Music composed for dancing the pavane.
etymology: From French pavane, from dialectal Italian pavana, contraction of the older padovana, feminine of padovano, meaning from the city of Padua (Italian Padova, dialectal form Pava).

definition: A slip of paper included with your pay that records how much money you have earned and how much tax or insurance etc. has been taken out.
A heavy thick yellow fog.
example: A man bumped into a lamp post during a pea-souper; he immediately apologised to it, not realising what it was.
etymology: From pea soup + -er (suffix meaning ‘person or thing connected with’);

definition: Very large terrestrial southeast Asian pheasant often raised as an ornamental bird.
etymology: From pea (“peacock”) + fowl. Compare Icelandic páfugl (“peafowl”), Swedish påfågel (“peafowl”), Danish påfugl (“peafowl”).

definition: Nocturnal gregarious pig-like wild animals of North America and South America.
etymology: From Kari'na pakira (“collared peccary”), from Proto-Cariban *pakira.

definition: Bird with strong claws and a stiff tail adapted for climbing and a hard chisel-like bill for boring into wood for insects.
etymology: Inversion of woodpecker. Application to white people is due to the perception that the woodpecker is a symbol of whites, whereas the crow or blackbird is a symbol of blacks.

definition: The part of the human torso between the neck and the diaphragm or the corresponding part in other vertebrates.
In a didactic manner.
In a pedantic manner.
example: These interpretations are called ‘schemas’ or, more pedantically, ‘schemata’.

definition: A man who has sex (usually sodomy) with a boy as the passive partner.
etymology: Borrowed from French pédéraste, from Ancient Greek παιδεραστής (paiderastḗs, “lover of boys”), from παῖς (paîs, “boy”) and ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”).

definition: An exhibition of pictures or objects viewed through a small hole or magnifying glass.
A form of igneous rock consisting of extremely coarse granite resulting from the crystallization of magma rich in rare elements.
etymology: From Ancient Greek πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “to attach, join”) + -ite

definition: A superior grade of black tea; grown in India and Sri Lanka and Java.
etymology: Unclear; possibly from Hokkien 白毫 (pe̍h-ho, “white hair”) or Hokkien 白花 (pe̍h-hoe, “white flower”). See Tea leaf grading#Etymology. Compare to Russian ба́йховый (bájxovyj).

definition: Transmitting light; able to be seen through with clarity.
example: A pellucid brook.

definition: A Basque or Spanish game played in a court with a ball and a wickerwork racket.
etymology: From Spanish pelota (“ball”). Doublet of pellet.

definition: A skin disease characterized by large thin-walled blisters (bullae) arising from normal skin or mucous membrane.
Admitting of penetration or passage into or through.
example: A penetrable wall.
etymology: From Middle English penetrable, penytrable, from Old French penetrable, from Medieval Latin penetrābilis.

definition: A small flashlight resembling a fountain pen.
A long flag; often tapering.

definition: Bounder.

Admissibility as a consequence of being permitted.

definition: A semisolid mixture of hydrocarbons obtained from petroleum; used in medicinal ointments and for lubrication.

definition: Of or relating to the bones of the fingers or toes.

definition: Small sandpiper-like shorebird having lobate toes and being good swimmers; breed in the Arctic and winter in the tropics.
